fixes.explanation: True, baker. Paul calls the command to honor your father and mother "…the first commandment with a promise…" It's a line from the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:12). The promise is coming in the very next verse.

That one's true, friend. Paul calls the command to honor your father and mother "…the first commandment with a promise…" It's a line from the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:12). So this commandment is the first one that comes with a promise.

True, friend. Paul says, "Wives, submit to your husbands as to the Lord." Those last four words are right there in the line: "…as to the Lord." He's got a whole picture coming to go with it, so hang on to your oven mitts.

Shepherd and flock is a lovely picture, friend, but it's not the one in this verse. Paul says the husband is the head of the wife "…as Christ is the head of the church…" So the comparison is Christ and His church.
That's the one. Paul says, "Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her" The love he points to is Christ's love for the church. That's a high bar, friend.

Isaac, Abraham's son (Genesis 25:19), did love Rebekah, his wife (Genesis 24:67). But Paul doesn't point to them here. He says, "…just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her" That's the picture he wants husbands looking at.

Jacob, Isaac's son (Genesis 25:26), really did love Rachel (Genesis 29:18). But that's not the comparison Paul reaches for. He says, "…just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her" So the example is Christ, not Jacob.
That's right, baker. Paul says Christ wants "…to present her to Himself as a glorious church, without stain or wrinkle or any such blemish, but holy and blameless." Glorious is the word he picks.

I see why you'd poke at that one, friend, but it's true. Paul says, "He who loves his wife loves himself." He's just said husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies, and a few verses later he adds, "…no one ever hated his own body…" So the love for his wife and the care for himself go together.

Respect is the word, baker. Paul says, "…each one of you also must love his wife as he loves himself, and the wife must respect her husband." Husbands are told to love, and wives are told to respect, both said plainly. That wraps up his words on marriage.

Peace is a nice thing, friend, but Paul doesn't give it as the reason. He says, "Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right." The reason is that it's right. Give me a reason that short and I can carry it anywhere, even on this gold base.

That's the promise, baker. Paul says, "that it may go well with you and that you may have a long life on the earth." Two things are named: that it may go well, and that the life may be long. Both are tied to honoring your father and mother.

Rome isn't in the verse, friend. Paul says, "…He who is both their Master and yours is in heaven…" The masters hear it directly: the Master of their slaves is their Master too. And that Master is in heaven, not in any city on the map.

Jerusalem isn't mentioned here, friend. Paul says, "…He who is both their Master and yours is in heaven…" Notice who he's speaking to: the masters. The One who is Master over their slaves is Master over them too, and He's in heaven.

True, baker. Paul says, "…there is no favoritism with Him." He says it about the Master who is both the slaves' Master and the masters' Master, and who is in heaven. It's a good line to end the passage on.
